The finding in one paragraph

The fraud team reports gross fraud losses, which fell again this year. Those losses are GBP 135k. The full economic cost of the detection engine is GBP 909k, because the engine also declines 99,807 genuine transactions a year and pushes 222,754 alerts into a review queue. The single largest line is not fraud at all - it is the cost of reviewing alerts that are, in more than 99 cases out of 100, genuine customers trying to spend their own money.

Precision with 95% Wilson intervals. R04 fired 133 times: its interval runs from 2.1% to 9.5%, which is why it gets an interval and not a point estimate.

The metric that decides retirement is not precision

It is unique catches - the fraud a rule finds that no other rule found. R01 HIGH_VALUE_ECOM has respectable-looking precision and 77 catches a year, and its unique catch count is zero. Every single fraud it stops is also caught by at least one other rule, so switching it off loses no detection at all and removes 11,669 alerts.

R07 ROUND_AMOUNT_CROSS_BORDER produced 483 alerts and no confirmed fraud at all in twelve months. The honest way to report that is not 'precision 0%' but 'the 95% upper bound on its precision is 0.79%'.

Why the causal design mattered more than the arithmetic

The obvious comparison - declined customers against never-declined customers - says a false decline increases spend by 536%. It does not. Customers get declined because they are active, and comparing them against inactive customers measures activity, not the decline.

The design that works compares customers declined this month against customers who will be declined three months from now, matched on segment and CRM spend band, over identical calendar weeks. That returns -8.1% (95% CI -13.4% to -2.7%).

A placebo test on an event 90 days earlier returns +11.3% rather than zero, so some upward bias remains. The reported answer is therefore a range, -8.1% to -19.4%, and the cost model uses the conservative end. The true injected value was -9.75%, inside the range.

What this analysis cannot tell you

  • The rules were reconstructed from published fraud typologies, not read out of a production engine. A real engine has scores and sub-conditions this does not model.
  • Above-the-line testing only. Lowering a threshold requires re-scanning transactions that never alerted, which is done properly in Project 2.
  • The behavioural effect is measured over 60 days. Anything that shows up after that - attrition, reduced product take-up - is not captured and would make the false-decline cost larger, not smaller.
  • The analyst review outcome is modelled at a 78% catch rate and a 6% false-decline rate. Real dispositions would replace it.
Synthetic data, generated to the structure named in the project brief and calibrated to published UK Finance fraud rates. Every figure is reproducible from src/ and every assumption is listed in outputs/tables/assumptions.csv. Not real customer data.
